gist: Asianometry traces how Intel's high-volume economics, Windows NT and then Linux (backed by Intel, IBM, Dell and Red Hat) displaced proprietary RISC/UNIX server vendors like Sun between 1993 and 2006. It argues UNIX lost on business model, while Microsoft's Active Directory lock-in let Windows Server survive and pass UNIX in revenue.

insights.claim: Intel tried to replicate its PC playbook in servers: high volume improves yield, lowers cost and funds better manufacturing, creating a lead rivals like AMD and Cyrix could not overcome.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Scale-driven cost curves were the structural weapon against vertically integrated vendors.

insights.claim: Pre-Intel, enterprise servers were vertically integrated proprietary stacks (Sun SPARC/Solaris, IBM POWER/AIX, HP PA-RISC/HP-UX, SGI) costing hundreds of thousands of dollars and locking customers in.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: The lock-in and high prices were the margin pool that commodity entrants attacked.

insights.claim: The Pentium Pro (5.5M transistors, 150-200 MHz) slightly beat the fastest RISC chips on some integer benchmarks, resetting perceived limits of a 'desktop' architecture and giving Intel its server wedge.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: A performance parity moment at far lower price opened the door to the low and mid server market.

insights.claim: In 1996 Windows NT 4.0 sales grew 85% to 27% market share per IDC, after NT Server sold only about 30,000 units in 1993 and 115,000 in 1994.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Persistence plus iteration let Microsoft ramp from disappointment to a real server base.

insights.claim: Intel and Microsoft had structural friction: Intel ships new chips every two years and wants software that sells them, while Microsoft ships Windows every three to five years and prioritizes backward compatibility for its install base.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Misaligned incentives pushed Intel to seek an alternative OS partner.

insights.claim: Intel shipped a 32-bit chip (386) in 1985 but Microsoft had no 32-bit consumer OS until Windows 95 in 1995, and Microsoft reversed on a 32-bit-only Chicago after Pentium Pro design was locked, hurting its desktop graphics performance.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Software lag repeatedly capped Intel's hardware value, so Intel feared the same for 64-bit.

insights.claim: Windows NT was portable (Alpha, PowerPC, MIPS), raising the fear that Microsoft could commoditize x86 into just one architecture among many.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Intel needed an OS it did not depend on a single rival for.

insights.claim: NT 4.0 supported only 4-8 processors per OS instance versus up to 64 on some UNIX variants, a ceiling that kept Windows out of the high end.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Scalability gaps in NT created the opening for Linux and UNIX to defend the high end.

insights.claim: Intel stayed OS neutral, later formalized as 'Port of Choice', to avoid Microsoft's wrath after investing in Red Hat; OS makers had to accept it because Intel silicon had no real alternative.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: A dominant hardware supplier can fund multiple OS ecosystems without retaliation.

themes.theme: Linux: GPL, distros and cost advantage

insights.claim: The GPL prevented companies from taking Linux code, adding changes and reselling it closed-source, thereby saving Linux from the fragmentation that afflicted UNIX and assuring contributors their work would not be locked away.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Copyleft was the mechanism enabling corporate co-development without a single owner.

insights.claim: Distributions let Linux be monetized like bottled water, and Red Hat made money from CDs, training and support despite not owning the underlying IP; its CEO compared it to ketchup, where anyone can make it yet Heinz holds 80%.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Open source value accrues to brand, packaging and support rather than IP.
insights.quote: Anyone with tomatoes, sugar and vinegar can make ketchup, yet Heinz owns 80% of that market.

insights.claim: Linux price gap was enormous: a Red Hat box about $50 versus Windows NT licenses of $150 to $1,100 and UNIX systems at $25,000 to $250,000 or more.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Order-of-magnitude cost differences drove adoption among budget-constrained admins.

insights.claim: Adoption was driven by reliability and source access beyond price, even with weak application support, no Microsoft Office equivalent and executive distrust of free software.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Bottom-up sysadmin adoption preceded executive acceptance.

insights.claim: By mid-1997 Linux had an estimated 3-5 million users, up from a few hundred in early 1992, and by early 1998 almost 20% of public web servers ran it.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Internet servers were the beachhead where Linux showed share before the desktop.

themes.theme: 1998: Intel and the enterprise embrace Linux

insights.claim: Intel's 1998 move came after requests from labs like Fermi to port math libraries and evidence from OEMs that ISP Linux demand was exploding; Andy Grove then pushed the company to act.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Customer pull, not strategy, first alerted Intel.

insights.claim: On September 29, 1998 Intel, Netscape, Benchmark and Greylock invested in Red Hat; a Benchmark partner on Dell's board then got Red Hat to Michael Dell, and Dell began preinstalling Linux in early 1999.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Major OEM endorsement put Linux on par with Windows and Novell.

insights.claim: Summer 1998 saw IBM adopt Apache and Oracle reverse within three days from saying it had no Linux plans to porting Oracle8, after a 900-person 'Future of Linux' panel; Informix, Corel and Computer Associates followed.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Application ports are the tipping point for platform adoption.

insights.claim: Microsoft reacted with the Halloween Memos, a Linux attack team, the 'Linux Myths' page and the sponsored Mindcraft benchmark showing NT 2.5x faster on file serving and 3.7x on web serving, but its ongoing antitrust trial constrained its response.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Antitrust scrutiny limited Microsoft's ability to strangle Intel's Linux investment.

insights.claim: Web, email and firewall workloads did not need SPARC, so scaling out Intel/Linux nodes beat scaling up big UNIX servers; Sun's attitude that any box was fine as long as it was SPARC became its problem.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Sun's embrace of open Linux ports undermined its own hardware premium.
insights.quote: It didn't have to be a SPARC box.

insights.claim: The dotcom bust accelerated the shift: Amazon's 2001 Linux transition cut costs by an estimated $17 million per quarter, and E*Trade compared a $250,000 Sun 4500 serving 300-400 users with a $4,000 Linux box serving 180, solved by buying two.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Downturns force cost-based platform switching, accelerating commoditization.

insights.claim: Linux 2.4 (January 2001) and the later 2.6 kernel (late 2003, up to 64 processors) closed multiprocessor scaling gaps, making Linux viable for mid-range and eventually enterprise workloads.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Kernel scalability work moved Linux from web edge to core enterprise.

insights.claim: IBM committed $1 billion and 1,500 employees to Linux in late 2000 under Lou Gerstner, and later subsidized migration with training, app porting help and discounted machines.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Incumbent vendors funded the destruction of the UNIX margin pool, including IBM's own AIX peers.

insights.claim: A four-Xeon Dell running Red Hat at $24,000 cost half as much as a comparable Sun Fire; in 2002 Linux server hardware revenue grew 63% while UNIX fell 11%, though UNIX was still $17B versus Linux's $2B, and Sun's average server price fell 31% by 2004.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Price-performance parity plus growth divergence marked the inflection point.

insights.claim: x86-64 (AMD Opteron in 2003, followed by Intel's Nocona Xeon in 2004) removed the 4GB memory ceiling, one of the last barriers to leaving UNIX for databases and simulations.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: AMD, not Intel's Itanium, delivered the 64-bit move that finished off UNIX.

themes.theme: Why UNIX lost, and why Windows survived

insights.claim: UNIX lost less because of technology than business model: vertically integrated kingdoms could not withstand Intel's high-volume economics, and Linux offered UNIX's capabilities without lock-in.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Horizontal, volume-driven stacks beat integrated proprietary ones once good enough.
insights.quote: it had less to do with technology than business model

insights.claim: Microsoft defended with Active Directory (Windows 2000), which Ben Thompson called one of the most valuable free products of all time, creating identity-based lock-in far deeper than an OS swap.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Identity and management layers, not the OS kernel, drive switching costs.

insights.claim: Contrary to predictions, Linux did not kill Windows Server: Windows matched UNIX revenue in 2005 and surpassed it in 2006, while Linux growth came from eating UNIX and new markets like supercomputing, HPC, web and cloud.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Linux and Windows split the UNIX spoils rather than fighting each other head on.

insights.claim: Residual UNIX (Solaris, HP-UX, AIX) persists in banking and healthcare where porting is too risky, showing a long tail of legacy lock-in.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (Asianometry)
insights.so_what: Legacy platforms decline slowly and keep harvestable revenue.
